Physical Geography: Landforms and Earth Processes

Erosion is the gradual removal of soil and rock by wind, water, or ice. Erosion differs from weathering in that weathering breaks material down in place, while erosion transports the loosened material elsewhere.

Plate tectonics explains the movement of the rigid plates that make up Earth's outer shell. Where two continental plates converge, the crust buckles and mountain ranges rise. Where an oceanic plate meets a continental plate, the denser oceanic plate subducts beneath the lighter continental plate, producing volcanoes and deep ocean trenches.

The water cycle moves water between the ocean, atmosphere, and land. Solar energy evaporates surface water, the vapour condenses into clouds, precipitation returns water to the surface, and runoff carries it back to the sea.

A river delta forms where a river slows as it enters a standing body of water. Because the slower current can no longer carry its sediment load, the sediment settles and builds new land.

The rain shadow effect occurs when a mountain range forces moist air upward. The rising air cools and loses its moisture as precipitation on the windward slope, so the leeward side receives dry descending air and often becomes desert.

Glaciers shape landscapes by carving U-shaped valleys and depositing moraines. The weight of the ice grinds bedrock, and the debris left when the glacier retreats records its former extent.
